text: The launch and ascent phase proceeded normally through maximum dynamic pressure. At approximately 58 seconds into the flight, tracking cameras observed a small plume of unexpected flame emerging from the aft field joint of the right Solid Rocket Booster. The flame rapidly expanded, impinging on the External Tank and the strut connecting the booster to the tank. At 73 seconds, telemetry showed a massive structural failure of the External Tank, resulting in a sudden, explosive release of liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen. The orbiter was instantly torn apart by extreme aerodynamic forces while the boosters continued flying uncontrolled.

During the atmospheric re-entry and descent phase, mission control observed a loss of sensor data from the left wing. Telemetry indicated a rapid sequence of anomalous temperature increases and the loss of tire pressure readings in the left main gear wheel well. Ground controllers attempted to communicate with the crew regarding the tire pressure messages, receiving a partial, cut-off response. Seconds later, all telemetry and voice communication with the orbiter were permanently lost. Ground observers tracking the re-entry path over Texas captured video footage showing the shuttle shedding glowing debris, followed by the catastrophic breakup of the vehicle.

The spacecraft executed its scheduled main engine burn to initiate the Mars orbit insertion maneuver. Telemetry received at the Deep Space Network indicated the engine fired at the expected time. As the spacecraft passed behind Mars, Earth occultation began, and the radio signal was lost as expected. However, the loss of signal occurred significantly earlier than the calculated trajectory predicted. Following the scheduled occultation period, ground controllers awaited the re-acquisition of the radio signal, but no signal was detected. Subsequent tracking efforts using multiple Deep Space Network antennas failed to detect any downlink, indicating the spacecraft was lost.

During the maiden flight of the Ariane 5 launch vehicle, the ascent proceeded nominally until approximately 37 seconds after liftoff. Telemetry showed the vehicle suddenly veered off its intended flight path, exhibiting an abrupt and extreme aerodynamic angle of attack. This violent maneuver induced severe aerodynamic loads that caused the launcher to begin disintegrating in mid-air. Separation of the solid boosters from the core stage was observed due to the structural breakup. Less than two seconds after the sudden swerve, the onboard automated flight termination system initiated the self-destruct command, destroying the vehicle at an altitude of approximately 4,000 meters.

During the translunar coast phase, approximately 56 hours after launch, the crew heard a loud bang accompanied by spacecraft vibration. Telemetry immediately indicated a sudden voltage drop on Main Bus B and a rapid loss of pressure in Service Module Oxygen Tank No. 2. Shortly after, Oxygen Tank No. 1 pressure also began dropping. The crew visually observed a gas venting into space from the exterior of the Service Module. Multiple warning lights illuminated, fuel cells degraded and shut down, and the Command Module lost its primary electrical power and oxygen supply, forcing an emergency power-down of the Command Module.

During the Earth atmospheric re-entry and descent phase, the Genesis spacecraft released its return capsule for a planned mid-air recovery over the Utah Test and Training Range. Radar and optical tracking acquired the capsule as it entered the atmosphere. However, ground observers and tracking cameras noted that the drogue parachute, intended to deploy at high altitude to stabilize the capsule, failed to deploy. Subsequently, the main parafoil also failed to deploy. The capsule entered a high-speed spin and continued its ballistic descent unimpeded, impacting the desert floor at nearly 200 miles per hour and severely breaching the science canister.

During a period of routine momentum management and gyro calibration at the L1 Lagrangian point, ground controllers observed anomalous telemetry. The spacecraft unexpectedly transitioned into an Emergency Sun Pointing Mode. Over the next several hours, operators attempted to recover the spacecraft's pointing, but telemetry indicated the vehicle's roll rate was increasing and attitude control was steadily degrading. Ground stations noted the spacecraft was losing its lock on the Sun. Eventually, telemetry showed a critical drop in power generation as the solar arrays pointed away from the Sun, followed by a complete loss of the downlink signal and communication.

Shortly after orbital insertion and separation from the launch vehicle, the spacecraft was commanded to power on its primary systems. Upon establishing contact, ground controllers observed highly anomalous telemetry indicating the spacecraft was spinning at a rate significantly higher than expected. Furthermore, temperature sensors in the primary science instrument showed that the solid hydrogen cryogen was rapidly sublimating and venting into space. Telemetry confirmed the instrument's protective cover had ejected prematurely. The continuous venting of the frozen hydrogen acted as a thruster, exacerbating the spacecraft's spin and depleting the entire coolant supply within days.

Following a nominal launch and initial checkout in low Earth orbit, ground controllers lost contact with the Hitomi X-ray astronomy satellite. Prior to the loss of signal, telemetry indicated an unexpected and rapid rotation of the spacecraft. Ground stations observed a sudden drop in communication signal strength. Shortly after, the U.S. Joint Space Operations Center detected multiple space debris objects in the orbital vicinity of the satellite. Optical tracking from ground-based telescopes observed the main satellite body tumbling rapidly, exhibiting periodic flashes of reflected sunlight, indicating the vehicle had suffered a catastrophic structural breakup and total power loss.

During the Crew Flight Test spacecraft's approach and rendezvous phase with the International Space Station, telemetry indicated anomalous behavior in the Reaction Control System. Mission control observed that several aft-facing thrusters failed to fire when commanded by the flight software. Additionally, sensors detected helium leaks within the propulsion system manifold. As the spacecraft maneuvered within the keep-out sphere of the space station, further thruster deselects occurred, causing degraded attitude control authority. The approach was temporarily halted while the crew and ground teams evaluated the telemetry before proceeding to a delayed but successful docking.
